metadata.title: Grammar rules extracted from An Elementary Grammar of the Coorg Language
metadata.author: Captain B. A. Cole
metadata.scope_warning: Historical description of the Coorg/Kodava speech recorded in 1867. Not a verified description of every present-day dialect. The book uses an old transcription and the extracted text contains OCR errors. Forms and rules marked medium/low confidence must be checked against page images and fluent speakers.

confidence_legend.high: Clearly stated in readable source text
confidence_legend.medium: Rule is stated but exact forms/transcription need checking
confidence_legend.low: OCR or source wording is unclear; do not use as a hard rule

syntax_note.source_claim: The author says the rules of syntax are identical with Canarese (Kannada).
syntax_note.caution: This is the author's historical claim, not an independently verified modern linguistic conclusion.

orthography_and_pronunciation.writing_note: The author describes the speech as primarily spoken, uses Kannada characters for the written language, and Roman letters to indicate pronunciation.

vowels.inventory: Short vowels, long vowels and diphthongs are distinguished.

special_vowels.name: half_or_silent_u
special_vowels.description: A special vowel quality compared by the author to the u in English 'creature'; he proposed marking it with a dot below the vowel.

special_vowels.name: special_dative_vowel
special_vowels.description: A vowel in the dative suffix compared by the author to French eu in 'queue'.

historical_observations.rule: The author says guttural consonants are unknown or unused in the dialect as he recorded it.
The author says the consonant corresponding to ha is not used and may be replaced by another consonant or an initial vowel.
The author observes that initial Kannada ha in some cognate words corresponds to an initial vowel in the Coorg form.
The author notes p and h are often interchangeable, and l and d (including sounds represented as li/ri in the old transcription) are sometimes interchangeable.

verbal_nouns.rule: A verbal noun is formed by adding an ending transcribed by the author as -vadu to a verb root.

compound_nouns.rule: Two nouns may be joined to form a compound noun.

historical_assignment.neuter: Animals and inanimate objects, according to the author's description

feminine_formation.rule: Some masculine nouns ending in the author's transcribed -ru form the feminine by changing/adding -ti.

number.people_counting: When cardinal numbers refer to persons, the source says a human-counting element transcribed as -alu is added.

declensions.overview: The author identifies five declensions, classified mainly by the ending of the uninflected (crude) noun.

classes.stem_ending: vowel read as e in the OCR
vowel read as a in the OCR
vowel read as i in the OCR
neuter nouns ending in a vowel read as e; author notes an inserted consonant in most oblique cases

forms: forms vary by declension and gender; OCR does not preserve the full table reliably
-geu (forms vary by gender and noun class)
-pakka (forms vary by gender and noun class)

gender_notes: Instrumental endings differ for neuter nouns versus masculine and feminine nouns.
The dative has more than one form; the source distinguishes a form used across genders and another used for masculine/feminine nouns.
The locative likewise has forms conditioned by neuter versus masculine/feminine gender.
cases.implementation_warning: Do not apply these as universal suffix replacements. The source gives five declensions and gender-conditioned paradigms. Store full verified paradigms for individual noun classes.

quality_nouns.rule: The source describes lengthening of the final syllable before the suffix in several oblique cases of neuter quality nouns. Masculine and feminine quality nouns generally follow ordinary declension.

adjectives.position: Adjectives precede the nouns they modify.
adjectives.relative_participles: Relative participles may precede nouns as modifiers; 'who' or 'which' is implicit.
adjectives.inventory_note: The author says there are comparatively few adjectives and that the gap is often supplied with participial forms.

comparison.comparative: No regular comparative morphology is described. Comparison is commonly expressed by adding an element transcribed as -kinji to a dative form.
comparison.superlative: The author also describes comparison against a group using a plural locative form with the same comparative element.

personal.note: The source provides full case paradigms and describes stem-vowel changes in oblique cases. Check exact forms against the page image.

demonstrative.plural_note: Plural forms differ by gender and are declined similarly to the corresponding remote demonstratives.

singular.meaning: himself / herself / itself depending on context

reflexive_reciprocal.usage: Used with reference to a preceding third-person noun or pronoun. The source also records plural use as an honorific second-person singular.

indeterminate.note: Nominative described as common across genders; declension differs between neuter and masculine/feminine.

numeral.declension: The source says numeral pronouns are declined like demonstratives, with a special plural formation.

quantity.source_gender_note: The author records quantity pronouns only for neuter gender.

examples.meaning: so much / as many as those
so much / as many as these

interrogative.declension: The source says interrogative pronouns are declined like demonstrative pronouns.

verbs.passive: The author explicitly states that a passive verb form is absent in the dialect as he recorded it, and that the active form is used instead.
verbs.root: The verb root is generally the same as the second-person singular imperative.

moods.infinitive: Impersonal; formed from the root with an infinitive ending that varies by conjugation.
moods.imperative: Root plus person/number endings. The source gives distinct first-, second- and third-person forms and plural forms.
moods.negative: Root plus negative personal endings. The source says the same negative form may be used with plural pronouns preceding it.
moods.affirmative: Simple affirmative tenses are formed from relative participles plus personal endings.

simple_tenses.name: future_or_contingent_future
simple_tenses.meaning: I shall/will do; author compares its sense to a contingent future

compound_relative_participles.note: The source gives these patterns for meanings such as 'is/will be doing', 'was doing', 'has done/will have done' and 'had done'. Person endings vary.

compound_tenses.rule: Present, past and future compound tenses combine the present gerund of the lexical verb with the corresponding present, past or future tense of iru. Perfect, pluperfect and future-perfect combine the past gerund with the corresponding tense of iru.

causative.rule: Generally formed by adding a causative element transcribed as -chiru to the verb root. In many verbs an inserted -pi- element occurs between the root and causative ending.
causative.exception_note: The author says there is no fixed rule for the inserted element and it must be learned by practice.

irregular_verbs.rule: Some verbs have irregular present/past gerunds and irregular present/past tense forms, often involving consonant changes attributed by the author to euphony.
irregular_verbs.instruction: Maintain an explicit irregular-verb lexicon; do not force every verb through regular conjugation templates.

sound_and_form_variation: The source records optional vowel lengthening and consonant doubling in some tense and participle environments.
The author notes that speakers may change the final vowel of first-conjugation roots and the final vowel of second-conjugation roots in speech.
The author notes a consonant may be inserted in the imperative of the third conjugation for euphony.
Do not generalize these alternations without checking the specific verb paradigm.

formation.rule: Adverbs are generally formed by adding an ending transcribed in the source as -uṭṭu / -uṭu to nouns and adjectives.

declinable_adverbs.rule: Some time and place adverbs are declined like singular nouns and take case endings.

postpositions.note: The source calls this category postpositions and lists forms that follow a noun phrase. It explicitly says some govern the dative case.

must_not_assume: Do not translate by word-for-word dictionary substitution alone.
Do not treat the historical transcription as a modern standardized Kodava spelling system.
Do not assume suffixes apply identically to every noun or verb.
Do not infer missing forms from Kannada or Tulu without labeling them as hypotheses.
Do not invent Kodava words when the dictionary lacks an entry.
recommended_runtime_steps: Retrieve dictionary entries for input words and likely inflected forms.
Retrieve only relevant grammar sections for each sentence: noun case, pronouns, verb conjugation, tense/aspect, negation or postpositions.
Give Gemini the source forms and examples and tell it to distinguish verified forms from uncertain forms.
If a word or construction is missing, return an uncertainty flag rather than fabricate a translation.
Store irregular verbs and noun declension paradigms as lexical data rather than relying on broad suffix guesses.
Have fluent Kodava speakers verify every rule and example before treating it as authoritative.
